Discrimination was assessed using time-dependent area under the receiver operator curve (tAUC) for 6-, 12-, and 24-month mortality. RESULTS: We included 950 and 766 patients in the training and validation sets (mean ± sd age: 83 ± 6 years/81 ± 6 years; men: 55%/59%; 6-month mortality: 27%/22%). The final G-CODE model highlighted five strong predictors of 6-month mortality: not having a caregiver, weight loss, comorbidities, an impaired 4-instrumental activities of daily living score, and an impaired timed-up-and-go test. The tAUCs of the model, including the G-CODE, age, cancer type, metastases, and treatment, were 82%, 78% and 80%. CONCLUSIONS: The final G-CODE score (range: 0-17) accurately predicts 6-, 12-, and 24-month mortality. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT02884375 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

title: Paediatric therapeutic development workshop on desmoplastic small round cell tumours
authors: Innovative Therapies for Children with Cancer (ITCC)
the Cancer Grand Challenge Protect team
abstract: The sixth Paediatric Therapeutic Development Workshop focused on desmoplastic small round cell tumours (DSRCT). Less than 20% of patients with DSRCT survive beyond 5 years and there is no targeted therapy for this disease, which represents an urgent unmet need for new therapeutics. High priority targets include the EWSR1::WT1 fusion protein, the oncogenic driver, and targeting a junction-derived neopeptide presented by HLA-A*03 and HLA-A*11 using a T-cell receptor (TCR) is a novel approach. Other targets (LRRC15, SSTR3 and SSTR5, NECTIN4, STEAP1 and mesothelin) require further validation. Targeting ERBB2/HER2 or claudin-6 by antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) and NTRK3 by a small molecule inhibitor are promising approaches and are currently being evaluated. Existing clinical assets targeting (in order of importance) B7-H3, the DNA damage response, androgen signalling, FGFR4 and STEAP1 are also high priorities for evaluation in DSRCT, but obtaining therapeutics for clinical trials is a barrier. In view of the rarity of DSRCT, a global initiative in preclinical and clinical research to establish international trials and collect data from patients treated in a harmonised form would benefit patients. Progress can be made by a combined approach of developing new agents whilst evaluating existing therapeutics in well-designed trials.

title: Retraction Note: Chromatin structure, transcriptional activity and DNA repair efficiency affect the outcome of chemotherapy in multiple myeloma
Preclinical efficacy of a systemically-administered, second-generation STING agonist that promotes anti-tumour immunity in combination with radiotherapy
abstract: BACKGROUND: As potent triggers of innate immunity, STING agonists hold promise as active immunotherapeutic agents for cancer treatment. Second-generation STING agonists, suitable for systemic delivery, are being investigated in preclinical research and have entered clinical trials. Here, the novel synthetic STING agonist, BI-1703880 (STINGa), was investigated for anti-tumour and immunological effects. METHODS: We used human and murine immune and tumour cells to examine the effects of STINGa in vitro, and preclinical cancer mouse models to investigate effects in vivo. RESULTS: We show that STINGa activates the STING pathway and results in a transient and dose-dependent upregulation and secretion of interferons and proinflammatory cytokines in vitro and in vivo. We show that intravenous administration of repeated dosing with low-dose STINGa is well tolerated. We report that radiotherapy (RT) and STING agonism synergises to generate innate immune cell and CD8+ T cell responses that control tumour growth. RT/STINGa upregulated PD-L1, PD-1 and CTLA-4 in the tumour microenvironment. Our findings show that combining RT/STINGa with immune checkpoint inhibitors further increases therapeutic benefit. CONCLUSIONS: Our data confirm STING as a therapeutic target in cancer and support the clinical development of BI1703880 STING agonist, thereby suggesting radiotherapy as a potential combination for enhancing anti-tumour efficacy.

title: Waiting times and determinants of delay for head and neck cancer in England—a population cohort study using real world data
abstract: Background In Head and Neck Cancer (HNC), even short delays in treatment can worsen prognosis. We used real-world data to quantify waiting times and identify patient, tumour and health service factors associated with treatment delay in England. Methods Using linked national datasets (Cancer Registry, Cancer Waiting Times, Hospital Episodes Statistics, Radiotherapy and Chemotherapy), we calculated waiting times from referral to first treatment (surgery or (chemo)radiation) and used multivariable logistic regression models to examine factors associated with delay. Results Of 30,506 patients, 43% experienced treatment delay ( > 62 days from referral). Long delays ( > 90 days) affected 11% of patients treated with primary surgery and 20% of those receiving primary (chemo)radiation. Non-urgent referral (30% of patients) was the strongest predictor of long delay (aOR 4.07, CI: 3.54-4.68). Additional risk-factors included initial assessment at non-specialist (spoke) hospitals, non-oropharyngeal cancers, and higher socio-economic deprivation. Conclusions Treatment delays in HNC are worsening, particularly for patients treated with primary (chemo)radiation. Referral route is the strongest determinant. Interventions should focus on optimising referral pathways, increasing awareness of HNC symptoms among the public and primary care, and acknowledging the different drivers of delay associated with surgery and (chemo)radiation therapy.

title: CXCL14+ fibroblasts promote development of IBD-associated fibrosis and cancer by interacting with SPP1+ macrophages via collagen IV secretion
abstract: Background The pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) involves chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, which predisposes patients to an increased risk of fibrosis and cancer due to prolonged inflammatory stimulation. However, the specific mechanisms underlying secondary gastrointestinal carcinogenesis in individuals with IBD remain poorly elucidated, particularly due to a limited number of studies conducted at single-nuclei level. Methods We investigated the dynamics and interactions of cell subtypes during the progression of IBD-associated cancers through comprehensive analysis including single-nuclei transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics, ecological dynamic modelling, multiplex immunohistochemistry, in vitro co-culture and in vivo animal studies. Results The results revealed that CXCL14+ fibroblasts, the primary source of collagen in the microenvironment, play a pivotal role in the inflammation-cancer transition. These fibroblasts progressively increase in abundance during this transition and secreted elevated levels of collagen IV. The increased presence of collagen IV promotes the recruitment and differentiation of SPP1+ macrophages. This interaction ultimately contributes to the development and progression of IBD-associated fibrosis and cancer transformation. Collagen IV, secreted by CXCL14+ fibroblasts, plays a pivotal role in promoting the transition from IBD to cancer. Inhibition of collagen IV secretion not only prevents fibrosis but also hinders the development of inflammation-cancer transition. Conclusion Our findings are crucial for understanding the mechanisms underlying IBD-associated cancer and developing innovative therapeutic strategies. During the inflammation-cancer transition, activation of the SOX4 leads to increased COL4A1/A2 secretion by CXCL14+ fibroblasts, resulting in enhanced collagen IV synthesis. Collagen IV binds to ITGB1/CD44 receptors on SPP1+ macrophages and activates EGR1/2 to promote SPP1+ macrophage differentiation, while upregulating S100A10 and ANXA2. Activation of S100A10 and ANXA2 promotes recruitment of SPP1+ macrophages, which contributes to immune escape and secretion of oncogenes, thus further promoting fibrosis and tumorigenesis. In addition, SPP1+ macrophages further stimulate CXCL14+ fibroblasts to secrete COL4A1/A2 via TGF-β1, forming a feedback loop that amplifies interactions in the tumour microenvironment.

title: Inhibition of ACSS2 enhances cabozantinib sensitivity by blocking TFEB-induced autophagic flux in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Background Cabozantinib, a promising tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), has recently been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, the objective response rate (ORR) of cabozantinib as monotherapy is low. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop cabozantinib-based combination therapy. Methods RNA-sequencing was used to analyse the gene expression alterations in HCC cells after cabozantinib treatment. A luciferase reporter assay was used to measure TFEB transcriptional activity. In vitro and in vivo studies were applied to assess the effect of cabozantinib in combination with autophagy inhibitors on HCC. Results Our results showed that cabozantinib induces autophagic flux, which protects HCC cells from cabozantinib-induced growth inhibition and apoptosis. Further mechanistic studies showed that cabozantinib upregulates Acetyl-CoA Synthetase 2 (ACSS2) and promotes its nuclear translocation, which subsequently activates transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB then binds to lysosomal and autophagy gene promoter regions, thereby promoting lysosomal biogenesis and inducing autophagy. In addition, the combination use of an ACSS2 inhibitor or chloroquine (CQ) enhances the antitumor efficacy of cabozantinib in HCC both in vitro and in vivo. Conclusion Our study proposes a novel molecular mechanism of cabozantinib and provides insights into cabozantinib-based combination therapy for HCC.

title: Spatial transcriptomic sequencing identifies lipid metabolism and mitochondrial respiration as central features of T cell excluded esophageal adenocarcinomas
abstract: BACKGROUND: The tumour immune microenvironment influences neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy success in esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC). Complete responders show higher treatment-naïve intratumoral CD8+ T cell levels before treatment than non-complete responders. Understanding mechanisms driving CD8+ T cells exclusion from the TIME is essential to improving outcomes. METHODS: We performed spatial transcriptomics on treatment-naive CD8-low and high EACs (N = 12). Regions of interest (ROIs) were selected based on tumour annotation by a pathologist. Cancer (CK+) cells and immune (CD45+) cells were analysed within the same ROI. Findings were validated using bulk transcriptome data (TCGA) and metabolic profiling (SCENITH) of fresh tumour specimen (n = 5). RESULTS: Whole transcriptomic profiling showed cancer cell clustering based on T cell infiltration. Cancer cell transcriptomes of CD8-low tumours exhibited reduced antigen presentation and upregulated lipid and mitochondrial metabolism, while CD8-high tumours showed increased cytokine signalling and apoptotic pathways. In CD45+ compartments, CD8-low tumours were enriched for the PGC-1α pathway, linked to mitochondrial biogenesis and immunosuppressive myeloid populations. These findings were supported by TCGA data. SCENITH confirmed mitochondrial dependence of macrophages in CD8-low tumours. CONCLUSION: Our results suggest that mitochondrial metabolism and impaired antigen presentation contribute to T cell exclusion in EAC. These findings raise the hypothesis that targeting mitochondrial metabolism in these cancers can modulate the anti-tumour immune response and thereby improve the response to chemoradiotherapy.

title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Ligand-independent activation of EphA2 by arachidonic acid induces metastasis-like behaviour in prostate cancer cells

Retraction Note: Statins, 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase inhibitors, potentiate the anti-angiogenic effects of bevacizumab by suppressing angiopoietin2, BiP, and Hsp90α in human colorectal cancer
Complete blood count-derived inflammation indices in colorectal cancer: head-to-head case-control and prognostic analyses with population reference intervals and external replication
abstract: Abstract Background Systemic inflammation drives cancer progression. We investigated the clinical utility of five routine complete blood count (CBC)-derived inflammatory biomarkers, neutrophil–lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet–lymphocyte ratio (PLR), monocyte–lymphocyte ratio (MLR), systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), in colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. Methods We performed head-to-head case-control and prognostic analyses of five indices in 2305 CRC patients and 78,281 health‑screening controls, with replication in 1031 CRC patients. Analyses included propensity score matching, Cox regression, restricted cubic splines, and Harrell’s concordance index. Population reference intervals were derived, and cross‑population transferability was assessed using the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). Results All indices were elevated in CRC patients and independently associated with survival. MLR retained diagnostic and prognostic significance in Stage I disease and was replicated. Dose–response trends were observed across quartiles, with non‑linear threshold effects for MLR and SIRI. Incremental prognostic gains beyond stage were modest. Reference intervals showed substantial overlap between CRC and healthy populations, limiting screening utility. NHANES comparison revealed non‑uniform transferability. Conclusion CBC‑derived indices demonstrated reproducible diagnostic and prognostic relevance, with MLR particularly informative in early‑stage CRC. Reference intervals contextualise abnormality but should not be interpreted as CRC screening or treatment thresholds.

title: Efflux transporter biomarkers and treatment sequencing in parp inhibitor resistance
Conformational heterogeneity: a fundamental mechanism of adaptive phenotypic plasticity and therapeutic resistance
abstract: Specific genetic mutations serve as clues to cancer emergence. However, non-genetic cell state shift mechanisms-such as the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-drive swift, reversible drug tolerance and metastasis. Unlike the slow process of acquiring mutations, this plasticity allows rapid, drug-tolerant cells to revert to previous states upon withdrawal of the drug, thereby driving pharmacological resistance. Insight into the evolution of cell states in cancer is critical for optimizing drug regimens. Here we propose dynamic conformational heterogeneity as an untapped fundamental driver of adaptive resistance. Proteins do not function as simple binary switches; rather, they exist as dynamic ensembles. Cancer arises when their conformational distribution shifts permanently towards an active state. Drugs operate by selecting specific (oncogenic) 3D conformer shapes and reverse-shifting the population back to a stabilized inactive state. Epigenetic dysregulation in cancer cells amplifies expression levels of these proteins, shifting the ensemble toward the oncogenic state. The increased abundance of the active state saturates the networks, overcoming feedback controls. We propose that effectively countering cancer evolution requires drug combinations that target oncogenic conformations at both molecular and systems levels, including adaptive phenotypic plasticity factors, shifting focus from individual static targets to dynamic population states.

title: A randomized clinical trial comparing visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) to Pocket Colposcopy for the triage of HPV+ women living with HIV in Kisumu, Kenya
abstract: Abstract Objective The World Health Organization recommends a “screen, triage, treat” approach for cervical cancer screening for Women Living with HIV (WLWH) in resource-limited settings, with Human Papillomavirus (HPV) testing preferred for screening. We assessed the use of the Pocket colposcope as an adjunct tool to Visual Assessment with Acetic Acid (VIA) for the triage of HPV+ WLWH. Methods We carried out a randomized clinical trial across six clinics in Kisumu, Kenya between November 2022 and April 2023 ( NCT04998318 ). WLWH who screened positive with self-collected HPV were randomized to either the VIA or Pocket arm. Exam positivity was determined by presence or absence of aceto-white epithelium (AWE). Directed biopsies were performed on AWE; if negative, two random biopsies were taken. Pathology was used to determine diagnostic accuracy. Providers and participants took brief surveys after each exam. Findings The rate of a positive exams was 17.3% for VIA compared to 14.3% for the Pocket. The overall rate of CIN2/3 was 15.4%, with 12.2% in the VIA Arm and is 18.8% in the Pocket Arm. Pocket and VIA performed comparably on all sensitivity, specificity and negative predictive value (NPV). For Pocket compared to VIA, Sensitivity was 26.3% vs 25.0%; specificity was 88.9% vs 84.0%; and NPV was 82.9% vs 87.1%. However, the positive predictive value (PPV) of the Pocket colposcope arm was almost a factor of two higher than that of the VIA arm (Pocket arm PPV was 375 is and that of the VIA arm was 20.6%). The Pocket Colposcope was acceptable to providers and patients for clinic-based triage of HPV positivity. Conclusion Provider assessment with the Pocket colposcope detected significantly more treatable disease, thereby reducing the need for overtreatment. This study indicates that the Pocket colposcope is a feasible, lower cost colposcopic device, which could facilitate biopsy-confirmation of disease, increase provider training, patient education and facilitate remote diagnosis.

title: Long-term fatigue based on the EORTC QLQ-C30 up to five years after radiotherapy and its trajectories in men diagnosed with non-metastatic prostate cancer in the international REQUITE study
abstract: Abstract Background Fatigue is a common symptom in cancer patients associated with impaired quality of life (QoL). Little is known about long-term fatigue trajectories in prostate cancer (PCa) patients. Methods Using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Group Core Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30), 1758 men treated with radiotherapy (2014–2016) for non-metastatic PCa prospectively reported fatigue up to five years later. Associations between pre-radiotherapy characteristics and clinically important fatigue (Score: ≥39/100) two years post-radiotherapy were investigated using logistic regression. Fatigue trajectories were explored using latent class growth analysis and multinomial regression. Results About 35% (608/1758) of patients experienced clinically important fatigue at least once from the start of radiotherapy up to five years later. Two years post-radiotherapy, 14% of patients reported fatigue, which was associated with pre-radiotherapy fatigue level (OR: 8.67), self-reported diabetes (OR: 1.94), BMI (OR: 1.07), and age (OR: 1.03). Long-term fatigue was strongly linked to pain, insomnia, pelvic symptoms, functional impairments, and reduced QoL. Four fatigue trajectories were identified, characterised by low (45%), moderate (42%), elevated and decreasing (8%), and (6%) increasing mean fatigue levels. Diabetes was associated with a 6 percentage point increase in the probability of experiencing an increasing fatigue trajectory. Conclusions The findings emphasise the need for early identification of PCa patients susceptible to long-term fatigue. PCa patients with elevated pre-radiotherapy fatigue levels and diabetes may require closer monitoring in risk-stratified aftercare programmes.
